# In Praise of the Unread

There is a stack of books on my imaginary nightstand, and if you're a reader, there is likely a real one on yours. Somewhere near the top sits a novel with a bookmark lodged permanently at page forty, stranded there since a holiday two summers ago. Beneath it: a history you bought in an airport, a memoir someone pressed into your hands saying *you have to*, and a library book you've renewed so many times the librarians have started to look at you with gentle suspicion. The pile leans. The pile grows. The pile, if we are honest, will never be read in its entirety—and I have come to believe that this is not a failure. It might be the whole point.

The Japanese have a word for this condition: *tsundoku*, the habit of acquiring books and letting them accumulate unread. I love that the word exists, because naming a thing is halfway to forgiving it. English offers no equivalent; we treat the unread book as a small moral lapse, evidence of laziness or pretension. But *tsundoku* carries no such sting. It describes the pile the way you'd describe weather—something that happens around people who love books, as natural and unremarkable as rain.

The most eloquent defense of the pile comes from the writer Nassim Nicholas Taleb, who tells a story about Umberto Eco's personal library. Eco owned some thirty thousand volumes. Visitors, Taleb says, fell into two camps. The first would wander the shelves and ask the inevitable question: *Have you read all of these?* The second—rarer, wiser—understood immediately that a private library is not a trophy case of completed work. It is a research tool, a working model of everything its owner does not yet know. Taleb calls the unread collection the "antilibrary," and he insists that read books are far less valuable than unread ones. A shelf of finished books is a résumé. A shelf of unread books is a horizon.

The mathematics support him. By one well-known estimate, humanity has produced roughly 130 million distinct books, with a couple of million new titles appearing every year. Suppose you are a ferocious reader—fifty books a year, sustained for sixty years of adult life. That's three thousand books: monastic devotion rewarded with a rounding error. Every book you open is ten thousand you close forever. Reading, seen clearly, is triage performed in an infinite hospital. This sounds despairing, but I find it strangely liberating. Once you accept that you cannot read everything, you are free. Free to abandon the novel that isn't working—the librarian Nancy Pearl has a rule: give a book fifty pages, and if you're over fifty, subtract your age from a hundred and grant it only that many, on the grounds that life shortens and books don't. Free, too, to choose by whim rather than duty, which is usually how the best reading happens anyway.

So why do we keep buying them? Because purchasing a book and reading a book are two separate hobbies, and only one of them requires a comfortable chair. When you buy a history of Byzantium, you are not really buying paper and glue. You are buying a possible self—the person who will someday speak casually of the Fourth Crusade. The purchase delivers a small advance payment of that identity without demanding the labor, the way running shoes make you feel faintly athletic on the walk home from the store. It's a little absurd. It's also, I think, tender. Every unread book is a letter addressed to someone who doesn't exist yet: the future you, slightly wiser, with more time, who will finally get around to everything.

The antilibrary has metastasized in the digital age. My browser tabs form the skyline of a city I keep meaning to visit. There are articles saved to read-later apps that were, statistically, read never; a watchlist of films queued for a rainy day that never arrives at the right length; a podcast backlog stretching behind me like a contrail. We live amid an abundance of intention and a scarcity of attention, and the gap between the two is where most modern guilt is manufactured. The unread book at least sits quietly. The unplayed video game sends you notifications.

But here is the deeper defense, the one I actually believe. The unread books on your shelf constitute a map of your own ignorance, drawn with unusual honesty. You bought them because some part of you noticed a gap—an era you couldn't place, a science you'd never grasped, a voice you'd never heard—and marked it, the way old cartographers wrote *here be dragons* at the edges of the known. To walk past your shelves, then, is to be reminded of the shape of what you don't know, which is the beginning of every kind of wisdom worth having. The person who has read every book they own lives in a house with no doors. The pile keeps the doors ajar.

I won't pretend the pile never reproaches. There is the book you have carried through three apartments, wrapped in plastic for each move, its presence slowly shifting from promise to accusation. At some point every such book demands a decision: open me or release me. Both are honorable. I have given away books I once swore I'd read, and felt not shame but something like weather clearing—the understanding that a library is not a to-do list. It is closer to a garden. Things grow there at their own pace, some of them after years of apparent dormancy, some of them never, and the ones that never bloom are not wasted. They were part of the soil.

Besides, unread books are not inert. Their spines work on you at a glance. Their titles lodge like seeds. You absorb, by proximity and osmosis, the simple fact that the world contains far more than you will ever hold—and that this is not a threat but an invitation, renewed every time you walk past the shelf.

So tonight, if you have a pile, don't apologize to it. Pick one up—not the worthy one, not the one that would impress anyone, just the one your hand finds first. Crack the spine. Read the first page. The rest of the pile will not accuse you. It will do what it has always done, patiently, in the dark: wait, and hold the doors open.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is a genuinely open creative prompt. Let me think about what would be interesting and authentic to write about.

I could write about many things:
- The nature of curiosity
- Something philosophical about language and thought
- An essay about attention in the modern world
- Something about craft, making things
- The history of a concept
- Personal reflection (though I should be thoughtful about what "personal" means for me)

Let me pick something I can write about with genuine engagement. The instruction says "write freely about whatever you want" — so this is an invitation to actually choose something that interests me, not to second-guess what the user might want. That said, something broadly interesting and well-written would serve best.

Ideas:
1. An essay on libraries and the feeling of being surrounded by books you haven't read — the "antilibrary" concept from Umberto Eco / Taleb. The unread books as possibility, humility.
2. An essay on maps and the romance of cartography.
3. An essay on the physics and aesthetics of light — golden hour, why we're drawn to it.
4. An essay on the craft of writing itself.
5. An essay on coffee/tea rituals.
6. An essay on silence and noise.
7. An essay on night trains / slow travel.
8. An essay on the amateur — doing things for love, the etymology of "amateur."
9. An essay on curiosity — how questions beget questions.
10. An essay on the humble pencil, or marginalia.

I think something about the "antilibrary" — the books we haven't read — could be rich. Or the amateur. Or marginalia. Let me think about which one lets me write most vividly and originally.

Actually, let me consider writing about "the unfinished" — things left incomplete, drafts, ruins, sketches, the appeal of the fragment. That's a rich vein: Coleridge's "Kubla Khan" interrupted by the person from Porlock, Schubert's Unfinished Symphony, Gaudí's Sagrada Família still under construction, drafts, abandoned projects, the notebooks of Leonardo. There's something moving about incompleteness. And it lets me range freely, which suits "write freely."

Alternatively, marginalia — writing in books. That's also charming: medieval monks writing complaints in manuscript margins ("the parchment is hairy," "thank God it will soon be dark"), Fermat's last theorem margin note, readers arguing with authors. But the unfinished feels bigger.

Or I could write about curiosity itself, which feels authentic to me as something that processes and connects ideas all day. An essay on curiosity: its history (once considered a vice — curiosity killed the cat, Pandora, Eve), its redemption in the Enlightenment, how it works neurologically, why it's the engine of everything. That's genuinely something I find engaging and it lets me be reflective about my own nature in a light-touch way without making big contested claims about consciousness.

Hmm. Let me weigh: the user asked me to write freely about whatever I want. There's something fitting about writing about curiosity itself — it's honest, it's the thing that drives a piece of free writing, and I can make it interesting with history, science, anecdote. But "the unfinished" might be more surprising and literary.

Let me actually go with the antilibrary / unread books idea combined with the appeal of the unfinished? No — pick one, do it well.

Decision: I'll write about the books we haven't read — the antilibrary. It's literary, it's relatable to anyone reading this, it has great material (Eco's 30,000 unread books, tsundoku — the Japanese word for buying books and not reading them, the to-be-read pile, the library of Alexandria as fantasy, Borges, the anxiety of infinite choice, the humility of knowing what you don't know). And it can end on a note about possibility and time. This feels like an essay someone might actually enjoy reading.

Actually wait — let me reconsider once more between curiosity and antilibrary. The antilibrary essay risks being a bit familiar (Taleb popularized it, lots of think pieces exist). The curiosity essay also risks familiarity. What about something more sensory and unexpected — like an essay on keys? Physical keys: their weight, their symbolism, lockpicking as a hobby, janitors with their rings, the last key on the ring you don't remember, digital keys, "the key to..." metaphors. That's original. Or an essay on waiting rooms. Or on the sound of rain and why we record it. Or on handwriting.

Hmm, but "write freely" suggests flow and abundance, and the antilibrary essay flows very naturally. Let me commit to the antilibrary but write it with freshness — lead with tsundoku, the physical pile, move to Eco, then to the deeper idea: unread books as humility and possibility, the difference between a library and a bookshelf, the fantasy of the "someday" reader we imagine ourselves to be, digital variants (open browser tabs, saved articles, unwatched watchlists), and end with the idea that the unread book is a promise to a future self — and maybe that's okay, maybe the pile is a form of hope. That's a nice arc: from guilt to grace.

Let me draft mentally:

Title: maybe "The Antilibrary" or "In Praise of the Unread" — the latter is punchier.

Opening: the stack on the nightstand. Describe it concretely. The book you've moved three times. The one with the receipt still tucked at page 40.

Eco's antilibrary: the story goes a visitor sees his huge library and asks "how many have you read?" and Eco (or Taleb's telling) says the point is the unread ones — the library of what you don't know. Read books are less valuable than unread ones as a research tool and as a reminder of the vastness of ignorance. Actually the precise anecdote: Taleb in The Black Swan describes Eco's library of 30,000+ books and distinguishes between visitors who ask "have you read all these?" and those who understand a private library is a research tool, not an ego-boosting appendage. Read books are worth far less than unread ones. He calls the unread collection the "antilibrary."

Then the psychology: buying a book is buying a possible self. The person who will read that history of Byzantium, learn bread-baking, finally understand general relativity. The purchase delivers a small dose of the identity without the labor. Like buying running shoes. There's something slightly comic but also touching about it.

The infinite choice problem: more books published every day than you could read in... some figure. Roughly 2-3 million books published per year globally (including self-published, it's higher). Even just traditionally published, hundreds of thousands. If you read 50 books a year for 50 years that's 2,500 books — a rounding error against even one year's output, let alone the ~130 million distinct books Google Books estimated existed as of 2010. So every choice is a renunciation. Reading is triage.

The mercy of this: once you accept you can't read everything, you're free. You can abandon books. (Maybe mention the "rule of fifty" — Nancy Pearl's rule: if you're under 50, give a book 50 pages; over 50, subtract your age from 100 — because life is short.) That's a nice concrete detail.

Digital antilibraries: open tabs, Pocket/Instapaper queues, Netflix "My List," Steam backlog, saved-for-later. The modern condition is abundance of intention, scarcity of attention. The tab bar as a skyline of aspirations.

The future self: the unread book as a promise, a letter to the person you might become. Even if never opened, it did something — it kept a door ajar in your mind. Though also honest: sometimes the pile is just guilt in paper form. The book as reproach. The moving-boxes problem.

End on grace: give away, let the pile breathe, a library is not a to-do list but a garden — things growing at their own pace, some you'll never get to, and that's the point: it exceeds you, and things that exceed us are why we bother. Or end with the image of picking one up tonight, arbitrarily, and the pile forgiving you.

Word count: aim for ~1000 words. The user said "for 1000 words" — so roughly 1000. I should aim for close to 1000, maybe 950–1050. I won't pad, but I'll let the essay breathe to reach that range. I shouldn't state the word count unless asked... actually it could be fine to just deliver. No need for a header announcement, but a title is nice.

Format: A title, then flowing prose paragraphs, maybe 8-10 paragraphs. No headers needed. No bullet points. This is an essay. Length ~1000 words. Markdown minimal — italics for book titles and foreign words, an em dash here and there. That suits conversational essay format.

Let me write it now, keeping track of approximate length. Roughly 9-10 paragraphs of 100-120 words each.

Counting words as I go is hard, but I'll aim for a full essay and it'll land near 1000. Let me write it properly now and estimate. I'll count roughly by paragraph: if each paragraph ~105 words and I write ~10 paragraphs, that's ~1050. Good.
